title: Counting the Most Beautiful Names
intro: Muhammad ibn Farhan al-Fayfi arranged ninety-nine names of God to help a learner remember them and use them in prayer. He begins with a saying transmitted by Abu Hurayra, then sets out groups of four and three, pairs and finally single names. A verse from the Qur’an brings him back to two things the worshipper can do with a name, praise God and ask him for something.

translation: Of God’s names there are ninety,
and nine more follow them.
1.sharh: The poet makes the listener do the addition. “Of his names” picks out the ninety-nine associated with a particular promise.

translation: Whoever takes account of them is rewarded with Paradise,
as is faithfully reported in the Prophet’s tradition
2.sharh: The reward gives the exercise its purpose. The sentence runs over to the next line for the name of the person who transmitted the saying.

translation: by Abu Hurayra, from the Chosen One.
May God bless him through the ages.
3.sharh: Abu Hurayra attributes the saying to Muhammad. The poet interrupts the lesson to send a blessing after the Prophet’s name.

translation: To account for them, count them, then understand,
then call on him, you who love knowledge.
4.sharh: Counting supplies the words, understanding gives them meaning, and prayer puts that knowledge to use. This order shapes the rest of the poem.

translation: O God, O Lord, O Most Merciful,
O Merciful One, we ask forgiveness.
5.sharh: The first four names form an actual prayer. Two come from the Arabic root for mercy, a fitting prelude to asking forgiveness.

translation: First and Last, you encompass time.
Manifest and Hidden, you encompass space.
6.sharh: These are the four names in Qur’an 57.3. The poet hears the first pair as spanning time and the second as expressing a reach from which nothing is hidden.

translation: In The Gathering come Holy, Peace, Giver of Security,
Guardian. In him I do believe.
7.sharh: The chapter title points to Qur’an 59.23. The Arabic word for the Giver of Security returns at the end with a human speaker, where it means “a believer”.

translation: The Compeller, the Supremely Great, know this,
and the Maker, the Shaper in the womb.
8.sharh: The first two names complete another part of the passage in The Gathering. The poet connects the Maker and the Shaper with Qur’an 3.6, where God forms human beings in the womb.

translation: You are the Sovereign, Owner and King.
I am the needy one who owns nothing.
9.sharh: Four Arabic words share the root for possessing or ruling. The last belongs to the speaker, who can claim nothing as his own.

translation: You are the All-Powerful, the Able, the Omnipotent.
I am weak and cannot win for myself.
10.sharh: Three related forms intensify the idea of power. The reply from the worshipper gives that grammatical exercise a personal stake.

translation: You are the High, the Exalted, the Highest.
I am the lowly servant in your charge.
11.sharh: The three names rise towards the superlative “Highest”. The same word that can mean a protector elsewhere in the poem here describes the dependent servant.

translation: You are the Generous, Most Generous, the Great Provider,
the Provider, Creator, ever creating.
12.sharh: Related names now come in pairs. The pair concerned with provision straddles the line break, drawing the voice on towards the two names for creating.

translation: You are the Bountiful Rewarder, the Appreciative, the Oft-Forgiving.
You are the Forgiving, the Subduer, the Supreme Conqueror.
13.sharh: God’s “thanks” to a worshipper means acknowledging and rewarding good. The other two pairs move from forgiveness to irresistible power.

translation: You are the Wise, the Judge, Patron and Protector,
the One, the Unique, each pair plainly akin.
14.sharh: Wisdom and judgement make the first pair, protection the second, oneness the third. The resemblance is between the meanings of the names.

translation: The Living, the Sustainer, the Truth, the Manifest,
the All-Hearing and All-Seeing, attentive listener.
15.sharh: The pairing now follows names that occur together in scripture. Life is coupled with sustaining other life, hearing with seeing.

translation: He is the Subtle, the All-Aware, the Praiseworthy
with the Glorious, the Watchful and the Witness.
16.sharh: What is too fine to notice is still known to God. The poet links praise to glory and watchfulness to witnessing, carrying the middle pair over the break.

translation: He is the Near, the Responsive, the Strong,
and the Mighty, prevailing over all who have strength.
17.sharh: Nearness is paired with answering the caller. The word for strength returns in the last phrase, this time describing someone subject to God’s might.

translation: He is the Decisive Judge, the All-Knowing.
He is the Self-Sufficient, the Forbearing.
18.sharh: In Qur’an 34.26 the “Opener” settles a dispute with full knowledge. Freedom from need and forbearance make up the second pair.

translation: In the tradition, the Modest and the One who covers faults.
That completes the coupled names, learned friend.
19.sharh: These names come together in a prophetic saying about modesty and concealment. The direct address marks the end of this kind of pairing.

translation: Of the names that face each other there are four.
The One who brings forward is also the One who holds back.
20.sharh: Four names make two contrasting pairs. The first pair covers giving something precedence and making it wait.

translation: Likewise, the Withholder and the One who extends.
All four are in the tradition, careful student.
21.sharh: Closing and opening a hand give Arabic its words for restricting and extending provision. The poet locates both pairs in prophetic tradition.

translation: The remaining names stand singly.
There are thirty, so complete the count.
22.sharh: The last thirty have individual places in this particular arrangement. The learner is asked to keep a running total.

translation: He is God, the Kind, the Accepter of Repentance,
the Beautiful, the Generous beyond reckoning.
23.sharh: “God” here renders the Arabic common noun for the one worshipped. The close appears to play on counting itself, as though generosity exceeded the learner’s tally.

translation: Reckoner and Preserver, with the Judge,
compassionate and gentle, full of goodness.
24.sharh: The first names suggest keeping account, preserving and requiting. The close turns to tender care, gentleness and the good that comes of them.

translation: He is the All-Holy, he is the Master.
He is the Healer of the sick, the Eternal Refuge.
25.sharh: The sick person makes one name tangible. The last name, known from Qur’an 112, extends the thought to everyone who turns to God in need.

translation: The Good, the Magnificent, the Pardoner.
He is known as the Great and the Firm.
26.sharh: Goodness, greatness and pardon are followed by two names for greatness and firmness. The verb “is known” recalls the lesson in learning who these names designate.

translation: The Doer of Good, the Setter of Prices, the Giver,
the Sustainer, the Bestower of Favours, the Helper of his people.
27.sharh: The striking “sets prices” comes from a report about a rise in prices. It stands here among names for giving, sustaining and helping.

translation: The All-Encompassing, the Unpaired and the Loving,
Trustee and lavish Giver. My count is complete.
28.sharh: Witr is the unpaired One. The sequence ends with the One entrusted with affairs and the One who gives freely.

translation: Glory to him who drew our attention and guided us,
saying in The Heights, “Call on him by them.”
29.sharh: The words from Qur’an 7.180 give the list its destination. “By them” means by the names the reader has just learned.

translation: Prayer as worship is praise addressed to him.
Asking for something needed is the prayer of petition.
30.sharh: The final distinction explains the opening prayer for forgiveness. Naming God can itself be praise, and the same name can introduce a request.

2.1.2.head: مُحصٍ
2.1.2.meaning: One who keeps count and knows what is counted.

3.1.1-2.head: أَبو هُرَيرَة
3.1.1-2.meaning: Abu Hurayra, a companion of Muhammad and a transmitter of his sayings.

7.1.2.head: الحَشر
7.1.2.meaning: Al-Hashr, “The Gathering”, chapter 59 of the Qur’an.

7.1.5.head: مُؤمِن
7.1.5.meaning: Giver of security. When the speaker uses the same word of himself, it means a believer.

7.2.1.head: مُهَيمِن
7.2.1.meaning: Guardian who watches over and keeps safe.

8.1.1.head: جَبّار
8.1.1.meaning: The Compeller, whose will prevails. The Arabic root also carries the sense of mending what is broken.

8.2.1.head: بارِئ
8.2.1.meaning: Maker, the One who brings creatures into being.

8.2.2.head: مُصَوِّر
8.2.2.meaning: The Shaper, who gives each creature its own form.

9.1.2-4.head: مَليك ومالِك ومَلِك
9.1.2-4.meaning: Three forms from one root distinguish possession, kingship and the fullness of royal authority.

11.2.4.head: المَولى
11.2.4.meaning: A master or a dependent according to context, here the servant.

13.1.2.head: الشَّكور
13.1.2.meaning: The One who richly rewards even a little good.

13.2.3-4.head: القاهِر والقَهّار
13.2.3-4.meaning: Both names convey prevailing power. The second uses an intensive Arabic form.

15.1.2.head: القَيّوم
15.1.2.meaning: The self-sustaining One who sustains all things.

16.1.2.head: اللَّطيف
16.1.2.meaning: The Subtle, a name associated with knowledge of hidden things and kindness to creatures.

18.1.2.head: الفَتّاح
18.1.2.meaning: The One who decides between disputants.

19.1.3.head: الحَيِيّ
19.1.3.meaning: The Modest, a name paired with the One who conceals in the report about covering oneself.

19.1.4.head: السَّتير
19.1.4.meaning: The One who conceals faults. Two pronunciations of the name are transmitted.

21.1.1.head: ذَينِ
21.1.1.meaning: “These two”, referring back to the preceding pair.

21.1.3-4.head: قابِض وباسِط
21.1.3-4.meaning: The Withholder and the Expander, two names applied, for example, to narrowing or widening someone’s provision.

23.1.3.head: البَرّ
23.1.3.meaning: The Beneficent, generous in goodness to creatures.

23.2.4.head: تَحساب
23.2.4.meaning: The booklet prints this unusual form. Its link to reckoning suggests generosity beyond counting, though its exact construction is uncertain.

25.1.2.head: السُّبّوح
25.1.2.meaning: The All-Holy, free of any imperfection. The name comes from the root used in the Arabic formula of glorification.

25.2.4.head: الصَّمَد
25.2.4.meaning: The One to whom all turn for their needs.

26.1.4.head: العَفُوّ
26.1.4.meaning: The Pardoner, who effaces a wrong. The verse lightens the name’s usual double final consonant.

27.1.2.head: مُسَعِّر
27.1.2.meaning: The One who determines prices, a name taken from a report from Anas.

27.2.1.head: مُقيت
27.2.1.meaning: The Sustainer, who apportions nourishment. The word may also describe one with power to preserve.

28.2.1.head: وَكيل
28.2.1.meaning: The Trustee, the one to whom affairs are entrusted.

29.2.3.head: الأَعراف
29.2.3.meaning: Al-A'raf, “The Heights”, chapter 7 of the Qur’an.

30.2.4-5.head: دُعاء المَسأَلَة
30.2.4-5.meaning: Prayer of petition, asking for a good or for relief.
